scenes.text: Syllabus four point five includes work done by a force. By the end, you can calculate work from a force and a displacement. And calculate work against friction and gravity.

scenes.title: A crate travels uphill

beats.text: Consider a crate being pulled steadily up a rough ramp. It slides along the slope without speeding up or slowing down.
The pull must overcome friction and the downhill effect of gravity. We will find how much work is needed against each resistance.

scenes.text: Consider a crate being pulled steadily up a rough ramp. It slides along the slope without speeding up or slowing down. The pull must overcome friction and the downhill effect of gravity. We will find how much work is needed against each resistance.

scenes.title: The full question

beats.text: Our crate has mass four kilograms.
It travels five metres up the line of greatest slope.
The ramp is thirty degrees above horizontal.
The coefficient of friction is zero point two five.
Take g as ten metres per second squared.
The pull is parallel to the slope. Speed is constant and contact is maintained. Only weight, pull, reaction and sliding friction act. Use the sliding model f equals mu R.
Find the work done against friction, and the work done against gravity. All the information is now on the diagram. Pause and picture the journey.

scenes.title: Only the parallel component does work

beats.text: Work measures the energy transferred by a force through a displacement. For a constant force, start with the general formula.
W equals F d cosine alpha. Alpha is the angle between the force and the displacement.
Here is an angled force. Replace it by its components. Only F cosine alpha acts along the displacement.
The perpendicular component has no displacement in its own direction, so it contributes no work. The normal reaction on our ramp does no work for exactly this reason.
Our pull is parallel to the slope, so its work is force times slope distance.
Work is a scalar, measured in joules: newtons multiplied by metres.
If the crate does not move, displacement is zero and mechanical work is zero, even if maintaining the force feels tiring.

scenes.title: Work against friction

beats.text: Return to our moving crate. First find the normal reaction. The pull has no perpendicular component, and the crate stays in contact, so reaction balances the perpendicular weight component.
R equals m g cosine theta.
Substitute four times ten times cosine thirty degrees.
The reaction is twenty root three newtons.
For sliding contact, friction f equals mu R.
So zero point two five times twenty root three gives five root three newtons.
Work against friction equals friction times distance. This is the positive amount needed to overcome friction along the whole slope.
Multiply five root three by five.
That is twenty five root three joules, approximately forty three point three joules.

scenes.title: Work against gravity

beats.text: Gravity acts vertically. The distance paired with weight must therefore be the vertical rise, not the distance along the ramp. Look at the right angled triangle.
Height equals slope distance times sine theta.
So five times sine thirty degrees gives two point five metres vertically.
Work against gravity equals m g h. It is the weight multiplied by the upward vertical displacement.
Substitute four times ten times two point five.
The work against gravity is one hundred joules.

The five metres belongs in the friction calculation because friction acts along the slope. The two point five metres belongs here because gravity is vertical. The direction of the force decides which distance to use.

scenes.title: By a force, or against it?

beats.text: Our answers are work against resistance: positive energy requirements. Work done by friction on the uphill crate has the opposite sign.
Work done by gravity during the climb is also negative.
Here is the check. The speed is constant. Does that mean every force does zero work?
No. Constant speed along this straight slope means the forces balance: pull minus friction minus m g sine theta equals zero.
Multiply by slope distance d. Pulling work is P d, and d sine theta is h. So positive pulling work cancels the negative resisting work.
The total work is zero, although the individual works are not. Reaction alone contributes no work because it is perpendicular.
What would change if the same path were travelled downhill? Friction would still oppose motion, so its work stays negative. Gravity would now help the motion, so its work becomes positive.

scenes.title: What to remember

beats.text: You can now calculate work from force and displacement: use the component parallel to the motion.
beats.caption: ✓ Calculate work from force and displacement

beats.text: And calculate work against friction and gravity. Match friction with slope distance, and weight with vertical height. Always state whether work is by a force, or against it.
